items.name: Readability
items.evidence: The only code is inline `python3 -c` one-liners; no script is left behind. Names like `raw_wal`, `fixed_wal` and `frame0_page` are clear, but `bytes([b ^ 0x42 for b in raw_wal])` never explains where the key 0x42 comes from.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: There is no re-runnable decrypt or extract script. The XOR, copy and SHM-removal logic is pasted into several one-liners ([18], [20], [27], [28], [31]). /tmp/backup is deleted with `rm -rf` at the end, so the run cannot be repeated.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: The key 0x42 is hardcoded. The final write ([31]) does not check the magic bytes after decrypting. `os.remove(shm_path)` and `rm -f main.db-shm` are run on a live DB directory. The backups are deleted at the end (`rm -rf /tmp/backup`).

items.name: Recovery method is principled
items.evidence: The agent saw the repeated 0x42 bytes in the header/frames and confirmed the key: XORing frame 0's page gave 'SQLite format 3'. It decrypted the whole WAL, parsed salts and checksums ([21]-[22]), let SQLite replay the WAL, and verified the result: 11 rows, plus the read-only re-check at [37].

items.name: Original evidence preserved before in-place repair
items.name_zh: 原地修复前保留原始文件
items.evidence: At [1] the agent opened main.db read-write with `sqlite3.connect` while the WAL was still encrypted. SQLite discarded it, and at [3] main.db-wal was gone. The backup was only made at [14], after the agent re-fetched the file from the docker image, so the original evidence had already been destroyed.
